svg.title: the framework guards what reaches the repository — clean commits and no secrets — the commit checks accept clean work and secrets never reach the repository
svg.text: the framework guards what reaches the repository — clean
Scenario: the commit checks accept clean work and secrets never reach the repository
Getting out of a secret block

g.text: Given a framework project has the commit hooks installed
A freshly initialized project already has commit checks turned on: init installed a
commit-msg hook, a script that runs before every commit message is accepted. The card proves
the hook is there, not what it says.
When a teammate clones the same project bare, with no commit hooks yet
A teammate clones the very same project from the folder next door — the framework rides
along, Taskfile and all. Yet git NEVER copies hooks on a clone, from any remote or path:
.git/hooks holds no commit-msg, so at this instant nothing guards their commits.
Then task dev:setup-environment turns the hooks on, exactly as the dev
container does on build
task dev:setup-environment is the one-time setup every clone runs (the dev container even
runs it for you when it builds): it checks the toolchain and finishes by installing the git
hooks. From here the teammate's clone is guarded exactly like the original — the next cards
commit from THIS clone.
When a developer writes a conventional commit message
A conventional commit message follows a fixed pattern: a short type word, a colon, then a
plain instruction — like "feat: add login page".
Then the hooks accept it and let the commit through
The commit-msg hook calls commitlint, which accepts the message because it matches the
pattern.

text.tspan: git commit --allow-empty -m "feat: dogfood the commitlint hook"

g.text: When a developer writes a sloppy commit message
"sloppy" is not one of the allowed type words, so commitlint is about to reject it.
Then the hooks reject it with their own explanation
commitlint blocks the commit and lists exactly which rules it broke.
Given a project protected by the framework's secret scanner starts on a
clean feature branch
A freshly rendered project, committed once and checked out on its own feature branch:
nothing to report yet.
When the developer commits ordinary tracked, untracked and ignored
files
Ordinary work: one file gets committed, another sits in the project without being committed,
and a third is listed in .gitignore so git skips it. The scanner must leave all three alone.
Then the scan finds nothing to report
scan-branch runs clean and prints "No secrets detected in branch commits."
When the developer accidentally commits a private key to the branch
A fresh project (its own branch history): a fake RSA private key lands in a tracked file and
gets committed like any other change.
Then the scan blocks it and names the leak
scan-branch fails and prints "Gitleaks detected secrets in your branch commits!"
When the developer commits a secret inside a secrets.yaml the scanner
used to ignore
A different trap the scanner used to fall into: its allowlist told it to skip every .env
file AND secrets.yaml, exactly the files where a real key or token is most likely to sit.
Here a private key is force-committed inside a file literally named secrets.yaml.
Then the scan blocks it too, now the allowlist no longer skips secrets
files
The scan blocks the branch and names the leak, just as it did for the .pem. The allowlist no
longer looks away from secrets.yaml or .env files (issue #182), so a secret parked in one
can no longer slip in unseen.
When the developer keeps a second secret out of the scan by gitignoring
the file it lives in
A fresh project again: the secret file is listed in .gitignore before it is ever committed,
so the scanner never even looks at it.
Then the scan passes silently, the ignored secret stays out of sight
scan-branch runs clean again and prints the same "No secrets detected in branch commits."
line — the gitignored key was never part of what it scanned.
Given a committed private key is blocking a fresh branch
A fresh project on its own branch with a private key already committed: the scan already
refuses the branch. This is where a stuck developer starts.
When the developer deletes the secret file and commits the removal
The obvious first reflex: delete the file and commit the deletion. It removes the key from
the latest version, but the earlier commit that added it is still in the branch history.

text.tspan: git rm tracked-secret.pem && git commit -m "chore: remove the secret file"

g.text: Then the scan still refuses the branch because the secret stays in its
history
The scan reads the whole branch history since main, not just the latest files. It still
finds the key in the commit that added it, so deleting the file did not help. This is the
trap.
When the developer rewrites the history with the framework's
clean-secrets task
task git:clean-secrets removes the file from every commit in the branch history, not just
the latest one, and rewrites the branch. The destructive-operation prompt is answered with
yes.
Then the scan comes back clean and the branch is safe to push
With the key gone from every commit, the scan passes: "No secrets detected in branch
commits." The branch the scan was blocking is safe to push now.

svg.text: Storyboard e2e · 21 steps · 21 frames · every frame is its own pixel baseline (tolerance: 0)
● Given — stage ● When — actions ● Then — proofs
